# Public Datasets

## ResStock 2025 Release 1 New

The updated dataset builds on the End Use Savings Shapes methodology, with 28 packages. New major updates include the additions of Hawaii and Alaska, electric vehicles, updated utility rates, HVAC demand flexibility, electric panel estimations, and improved geothermal heat pump modeling. For details about the ResStock model used to create this dataset, see the Technical Reference Guide and the short readme paper which has a description of all packages, important assumptions, and changes from the last dataset release. A summary of how column names have changed in this dataset since 2024 Release 2 is also available. The geothermal heat pump results from this AMY 2018 2025 Release 1 dataset are shown in the Evaluating Geothermal Performance for the U.S. Building Stock Tableau dashboard with ComStock geothermal heat pump results.

For more information on this dataset, and other ResStock datasets, see our User Resource Website which has examples, FAQs, measure documentation and more. Have additional questions or comments? Email our team at ResStock@nlr.gov.

Dual Fuel Heating System  
Accessing Results 
This documentation covers the “Dual Fuel Heating System” measure upgrade methodology and 
briefly discusses key results. All results can be accessed on the ResStock™ Open Energy Data 
Initiative End-Use Load Profiles for the U.S. Building Stock Data Lake and on the data viewer at 
resstock.nlr.gov/datasets. 
Measure Summary 
Measure Title 
Dual Fuel Heating System Measure Upgrade 
Measure 
Definition 
This upgrade measure replaces any existing heating and air conditioning system 
with a dual fuel heating system that includes an air-source heat pump and a natural 
gas furnace. If the unit does not have air conditioning, it will receive air conditioning 
through the air-source heat pump. The technology applied in this measure upgrade 
package is denoted in ResStock as follows:  
• 
Dual Fuel Heating System, 92% Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency (AFUE), 
Climate Zones (CZ) 1–4 
• 
Dual Fuel Heating System, 95% AFUE, CZ 5–8. 
Applicability 
This measure applies to all dwellings with: 
• 
Ducted non-shared (in-unit) HVAC with any of the following heating fuels: 
electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane 
• 
Have at least one appliance or an HVAC system fueled by natural gas. 
With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to 44.7% of the 
existing dwelling units. 
Not Applicable 
This measure does not apply to dwelling units with the following: 
• 
Shared HVAC 
• 
Non-ducted non-shared HVAC 
• 
Heating Fuel of None, Other Fuel, or Wood. 
These constraints exclude 44.3% of the dwelling units from receiving this measure 
upgrade.

### ResStock and ComStock

#### Overview

ResStock and ComStock (together called BuildStock) are highly granular, bottom-up models of the U.S. building stock that use multiple public and private data sources, statistical sampling, and sub-hourly building physics simulations to evaluate the potential impacts of building technologies on energy use, operational costs, emissions, comfort, and resilience. ResStock and ComStock annual and timeseries outputs are regularly published as standard dataset releases (SDR)^{[ref-type: bibr] 36,[ref-type: bibr] 37}. These datasets represent the baseline building stock and the application of upgrades to eligible buildings. BSS simulations are consistent with ComStock 2024 Release 2 and ResStock 2024 Release 2, as further described in the disaggregation section.

A brief summary of the workflow used by ResStock and ComStock is as follows:

  1. Using a variety of public and private data sources, a database of housing unit (ResStock) or building (ComStock) characteristics with conditional probability distributions is developed.
The fraction of annual hours that dual-fuel measures rely on existing equipment for backup is defined in Scout based on simulated hourly data for analogous dual-fuel measures in the BuildStock SDR datasets^{[ref-type: bibr] 8,[ref-type: bibr] 9}. These fractions are broken out by the state and by the equipment class and fuel type of the baseline equipment that the dual-fuel measure replaces.

Residential technology and fuel switching measures may both require costly upgrades to existing electrical infrastructure in order to support the switch. These additional infrastructure costs, which are reflected in the BTB dataset, include the cost of upgrading an existing breaker panel to 200-225A service, as well as the cost of installing a new 240V circuit where necessary to service new equipment upgrades. For the BSS forecast, we incorporated recent ResStock-based estimates of what portion of existing U.S. homes in each state that switch from a given type of baseline heating equipment and fuel type would require an electrical panel upgrade^{[ref-type: bibr] 35}. For FS measures, we furthermore assumed that electric equipment in the two highest tiers of performance (best available and breakthrough) and dual-fuel heating measures avoid the need for and cost of a panel upgrade. The installation of a circuit breaker to accommodate the new electric load is assumed regardless of FS measure performance characteristics.

#### Demand flexibility

DF measures shed or shift hourly residential and commercial electric loads in response to grid system needs, which are represented in our measure definitions by the net system load shape — total hourly system electricity demand minus variable renewable generation. Here we describe the key operational assumptions behind these residential and commercial DF measures.

## ResStock 2025 Release 1 New

The updated dataset builds on the End Use Savings Shapes methodology, with 28 packages. New major updates include the additions of Hawaii and Alaska, electric vehicles, updated utility rates, HVAC demand flexibility, electric panel estimations, and improved geothermal heat pump modeling. For details about the ResStock model used to create this dataset, see the Technical Reference Guide and the short readme paper which has a description of all packages, important assumptions, and changes from the last dataset release. A summary of how column names have changed in this dataset since 2024 Release 2 is also available. The geothermal heat pump results from this AMY 2018 2025 Release 1 dataset are shown in the Evaluating Geothermal Performance for the U.S. Building Stock Tableau dashboard with ComStock geothermal heat pump results.

Dual Fuel Heating System  
Accessing Results 
This documentation covers the “Dual Fuel Heating System” measure upgrade methodology and 
briefly discusses key results. All results can be accessed on the ResStock™ Open Energy Data 
Initiative End-Use Load Profiles for the U.S. Building Stock Data Lake and on the data viewer at 
resstock.nlr.gov/datasets. 
Measure Summary 
Measure Title 
Dual Fuel Heating System Measure Upgrade 
Measure 
Definition 
This upgrade measure replaces any existing heating and air conditioning system 
with a dual fuel heating system that includes an air-source heat pump and a natural 
gas furnace. If the unit does not have air conditioning, it will receive air conditioning 
through the air-source heat pump. The technology applied in this measure upgrade 
package is denoted in ResStock as follows:  
• 
Dual Fuel Heating System, 92% Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency (AFUE), 
Climate Zones (CZ) 1–4 
• 
Dual Fuel Heating System, 95% AFUE, CZ 5–8. 
Applicability 
This measure applies to all dwellings with: 
• 
Ducted non-shared (in-unit) HVAC with any of the following heating fuels: 
electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane 
• 
Have at least one appliance or an HVAC system fueled by natural gas. 
With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to 44.7% of the 
existing dwelling units. 
Not Applicable 
This measure does not apply to dwelling units with the following: 
• 
Shared HVAC 
• 
Non-ducted non-shared HVAC 
• 
Heating Fuel of None, Other Fuel, or Wood. 
These constraints exclude 44.3% of the dwelling units from receiving this measure 
upgrade.

### ResStock and ComStock

#### Overview

ResStock and ComStock (together called BuildStock) are highly granular, bottom-up models of the U.S. building stock that use multiple public and private data sources, statistical sampling, and sub-hourly building physics simulations to evaluate the potential impacts of building technologies on energy use, operational costs, emissions, comfort, and resilience. ResStock and ComStock annual and timeseries outputs are regularly published as standard dataset releases (SDR)^{[ref-type: bibr] 36,[ref-type: bibr] 37}. These datasets represent the baseline building stock and the application of upgrades to eligible buildings. BSS simulations are consistent with ComStock 2024 Release 2 and ResStock 2024 Release 2, as further described in the disaggregation section.

A brief summary of the workflow used by ResStock and ComStock is as follows:

  1. Using a variety of public and private data sources, a database of housing unit (ResStock) or building (ComStock) characteristics with conditional probability distributions is developed.
The fraction of annual hours that dual-fuel measures rely on existing equipment for backup is defined in Scout based on simulated hourly data for analogous dual-fuel measures in the BuildStock SDR datasets^{[ref-type: bibr] 8,[ref-type: bibr] 9}. These fractions are broken out by the state and by the equipment class and fuel type of the baseline equipment that the dual-fuel measure replaces.

Residential technology and fuel switching measures may both require costly upgrades to existing electrical infrastructure in order to support the switch. These additional infrastructure costs, which are reflected in the BTB dataset, include the cost of upgrading an existing breaker panel to 200-225A service, as well as the cost of installing a new 240V circuit where necessary to service new equipment upgrades. For the BSS forecast, we incorporated recent ResStock-based estimates of what portion of existing U.S. homes in each state that switch from a given type of baseline heating equipment and fuel type would require an electrical panel upgrade^{[ref-type: bibr] 35}. For FS measures, we furthermore assumed that electric equipment in the two highest tiers of performance (best available and breakthrough) and dual-fuel heating measures avoid the need for and cost of a panel upgrade. The installation of a circuit breaker to accommodate the new electric load is assumed regardless of FS measure performance characteristics.

#### Demand flexibility

DF measures shed or shift hourly residential and commercial electric loads in response to grid system needs, which are represented in our measure definitions by the net system load shape — total hourly system electricity demand minus variable renewable generation. Here we describe the key operational assumptions behind these residential and commercial DF measures.

L315@P12: 1.2.1.4 Capacity Retention
L316@P12: As outdoor temperatures drop below the rated capacity temperature of 47°F, the available
L317@P12: capacity of the ASHP decreases. The capacity retained by an ASHP below this temperature is
L318@P12: defined by its capacity retention fraction. This ASHP option’s capacity retention fraction is 0.5 at
L319@P12: 5°F. This capacity retention factor specifies the fraction of the ASHP’s rated capacity available
L320@P12: at 5°F. For this ducted ASHP option, its capacity at 47°F—equal to the ACCA Manual J cooling
L321@P12: load with ACCA Manual S oversizing allowances added—will be reduced by half at 5°F.
L322@P12: 1.2.1.5 Backup System and Switchover Temperature
L323@P12: This modeled ASHP option uses a natural gas furnace as its backup system. Fossil fuel furnaces
L324@P12: and ASHP dual fuel systems cannot provide heating at the same time. Therefore, a switchover
L325@P12: temperature must be defined for the ASHP system to switch over to the fossil fuel furnace to
L326@P12: fully meet the heating load. To operate this system economically, the switchover temperature is
L327@P12: typically set between 25°F and 45°F (Air Source Heat Pump Collaborative 2023). The ideal
L328@P12: switchover temperature depends on the efficiencies of the ASHP and furnace systems as well as
L329@P12: the prices of electricity and fossil fuel. Lennox recommends a switchover temperature of around
L330@P12: 35°F for its products (Lennox 2016). For this measure upgrade, the switchover temperature is
L331@P12: also set at 35°F.
L332@P12: 1.2.1.6 Duct Considerations
L333@P12: With this dual fuel system measure upgrade, there are some circumstances where the ducts in the
L334@P12: dwelling are resized when the upgrade option is applied. This occurs if the existing ducts are not
L335@P12: large enough to accommodate the ACCA Manual S-sized ASHP being installed. Because ACCA
L336@P12: Manual S sized systems are smaller than systems sized for the full heating load of the dwelling,
L337@P12: there is less likelihood that duct systems will be resized in this particular measure upgrade.
L338@P12: 1.2.1.7 Cooling Levels
L339@P12: This measure upgrade is intended to replace existing heating systems, but all dwellings that
L340@P12: receive this dual fuel option will also receive whole-home cooling from the ASHP, regardless of
L341@P12: whether the dwelling had cooling in the baseline. This will increase cooling energy consumption
L342@P12: in dwellings that were not already fully cooled, but it will also provide greater comfort and safety
L343@P12: in the simulated homes.
L344@P12: 1.2.1.8 Electrical Requirements
L345@P12: This section summarizes the electrical information for the dual fuel heat pump upgrade.
L346@P12: Electrical information in ResStock is used to assess whether the home’s electrical panel would
L347@P12: become space-constrained or over-capacity due to this upgrade. Section 3.3 describes the
L348@P12: electrical panel constraint modeling in more detail.

L350@P12: compressor, the air handler, and any electric backup allowed to operate simultaneously, as
L351@P12: summarized in Table 1. The heat pump compressor power rating is estimated based on its design
L352@P12: heating capacity using a regression equation derived from product labels. The air handler power
L353@P12: rating is estimated from the design airflow rate and the OS-HPXML assumption of fan power.

L315@P12: 1.2.1.4 Capacity Retention
L316@P12: As outdoor temperatures drop below the rated capacity temperature of 47°F, the available
L317@P12: capacity of the ASHP decreases. The capacity retained by an ASHP below this temperature is
L318@P12: defined by its capacity retention fraction. This ASHP option’s capacity retention fraction is 0.5 at
L319@P12: 5°F. This capacity retention factor specifies the fraction of the ASHP’s rated capacity available
L320@P12: at 5°F. For this ducted ASHP option, its capacity at 47°F—equal to the ACCA Manual J cooling
L321@P12: load with ACCA Manual S oversizing allowances added—will be reduced by half at 5°F.
L322@P12: 1.2.1.5 Backup System and Switchover Temperature
L323@P12: This modeled ASHP option uses a natural gas furnace as its backup system. Fossil fuel furnaces
L324@P12: and ASHP dual fuel systems cannot provide heating at the same time. Therefore, a switchover
L325@P12: temperature must be defined for the ASHP system to switch over to the fossil fuel furnace to
L326@P12: fully meet the heating load. To operate this system economically, the switchover temperature is
L327@P12: typically set between 25°F and 45°F (Air Source Heat Pump Collaborative 2023). The ideal
L328@P12: switchover temperature depends on the efficiencies of the ASHP and furnace systems as well as
L329@P12: the prices of electricity and fossil fuel. Lennox recommends a switchover temperature of around
L330@P12: 35°F for its products (Lennox 2016). For this measure upgrade, the switchover temperature is
L331@P12: also set at 35°F.
L332@P12: 1.2.1.6 Duct Considerations
L333@P12: With this dual fuel system measure upgrade, there are some circumstances where the ducts in the
L334@P12: dwelling are resized when the upgrade option is applied. This occurs if the existing ducts are not
L335@P12: large enough to accommodate the ACCA Manual S-sized ASHP being installed. Because ACCA
L336@P12: Manual S sized systems are smaller than systems sized for the full heating load of the dwelling,
L337@P12: there is less likelihood that duct systems will be resized in this particular measure upgrade.

L339@P12: This measure upgrade is intended to replace existing heating systems, but all dwellings that
L340@P12: receive this dual fuel option will also receive whole-home cooling from the ASHP, regardless of
L341@P12: whether the dwelling had cooling in the baseline. This will increase cooling energy consumption
L342@P12: in dwellings that were not already fully cooled, but it will also provide greater comfort and safety
L343@P12: in the simulated homes.
